Situation1: You just realized a comment you made has deeply hurt your friend's feelings, and you need to call them right now to apologize and clear the air.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They raise concerns about a policy that seems to disadvantage certain youth, seniors, or refugee applicants.
Story: I stared at my phone, my heart pounding. Just an hour ago, I’d made a careless joke at lunch, and now I’d learned from a mutual friend that it had really hurt Jamie. As a friend, I knew I needed to call Jamie right away, apologize, and talk things through. That’s what friends do—communicate, clear the air, and make things right. But at the same time, my inbox pinged with an urgent message from the youth center. The director wanted me to speak up at tonight’s council meeting about a new policy that would make it even harder for refugee teens to access after-school programs. As an advocate, I was expected to challenge these unfair systems, to be a voice for those who couldn’t be there themselves. Both roles demanded my immediate attention, but I only had so much time and emotional energy. My thumb hovered over Jamie’s contact, while my laptop screen glowed with the policy notes I needed to review. I felt torn, guilt and responsibility pulling me in opposite directions, unsure which call to make first.
